{{Short description|Theorem about prime numbers}}
In [[number theory]], '''Maier's theorem''' is a theorem due to [[Helmut Maier]] about the numbers of [[Prime number|prime]]s in short intervals for which [[Cramér model|Cramér's probabilistic model of primes]] gives a wrong answer.

The theorem states{{sfnp|Maier|1985}} that if <math>\pi</math> is the [[prime-counting function]] and <math>\lambda > 1</math>, then

:<math>\frac{\pi(x+(\log x)^\lambda)-\pi(x)}{(\log x)^{\lambda-1}}</math>

does not have a limit as <math>x</math> tends to infinity; more precisely the [[limit superior]] is greater than 1, and the limit inferior is less than 1. The Cramér model of primes predicts incorrectly that it has limit 1 when <math>\lambda \geq 2</math> (using the [[Borel–Cantelli lemma]]).

==Proofs==
Maier proved his theorem using [[Alexander Buchstab|Buchstab]]'s equivalent for the counting function of quasi-primes (set of numbers without prime factors lower to bound <math>z = x^{1/u}</math>, with <math>u</math> fixed). He also used an equivalent of the number of primes in arithmetic progressions of sufficient length due to [[Patrick X. Gallagher|Gallagher]].

[[János Pintz]] gave another proof,{{sfnp|Pintz|2007}} and also showed that most probabilistic models of primes incorrectly predict the [[mean square error]]

:<math>\int_2^Y\!\bigg(\sum_{2<p\le x} \log p -\!\sum_{2<n\le x}1\bigg)^2dx</math>

of one version of the [[prime number theorem]].
